title: Pointer methods and the method set
question: A type has one method with a pointer receiver. Does a value of that type satisfy an interface that needs the method?
answer: No. The method set of T holds only value-receiver methods; the method set of *T holds both. Calling c.Inc() on an addressable variable works because Go rewrites it to (&c).Inc(), but a T stored in an interface is a copy that is not addressable, so T does not implement the interface and *T does.
watch: Watch the interface box: storing c copies the struct, while storing &c holds a pointer to the original, so only the second Inc changes c.
expected:
1
Counter is Incer: false
*Counter is Incer: true
2

title: Go passes everything by value
question: Is Go pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? What happens when you pass a pointer?
answer: Go always passes by value: the callee gets a copy of every argument. A pointer argument is a copy of the address, so writing through it (*p = 100) changes the caller's variable, but pointing the copy somewhere else (p = &x) does not affect the caller's pointer.
watch: Watch the two frames: reassign changes only its own p, while write follows the arrow back into main's n.

title: new does not mean heap
question: Does new(T) or &T{} always allocate on the heap?
answer: No. Where a value lives is decided by the compiler's escape analysis, not by the syntax. A new(Point) that never outlives its function can stay on the stack, while a plain local whose address is returned is moved to the heap because the pointer outlives the frame. go build -gcflags=-m shows the decisions ("does not escape", "moved to heap: p"); gothik draws a simplified version of the same rule.
watch: Watch where each Point is drawn: the one from new stays in local's frame, the one returned by leak sits on the heap after its frame is gone.

title: Closures capture variables, not values
question: What does a closure capture, and why does this counter keep its state between calls?
answer: A closure captures the variables it refers to, not a snapshot of their values. Each call to counter creates a new n, and the returned function keeps a reference to it, so n outlives counter's frame (the compiler moves it to the heap) and each counter has its own independent n.
watch: Watch n leave counter's frame for the heap, and the two closures point at two different n cells.

title: Appending inside a function
question: A function appends to a slice parameter. Why does the caller not see the new element?
answer: A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) passed by value. When there is spare capacity, append writes into the shared backing array, so element writes are visible to the caller, but the longer length lives only in the callee's copy of the header. Return the new slice (s = add(s)) or pass a pointer to it.
watch: Watch both headers point at the same array: the 4 lands in slot 3, but main's len stays 3 until it reslices.

title: Struct copies are shallow
question: Is assigning one struct to another a deep copy?
answer: No, it copies each field's value. A string or int field is independent afterwards, but a slice field copies only the slice header, so both structs still point at the same backing array. A deep copy needs an explicit copy of the slice, for example with slices.Clone or make plus copy.
watch: Watch b get its own Name but a Scores header that points at the same array as a.

title: Maps passed to functions
question: If you pass a map to a function and it adds a key, does the caller see it? What if the function assigns a new map?
answer: A map value is a pointer to the runtime's hash table, and that pointer is copied into the function. Adding a key through the copy changes the shared table, so the caller sees it. Assigning a new map to the parameter only repoints the local copy and the caller is unaffected.
watch: Watch fill write into the one table main owns, while reset builds a second table that is dropped when it returns.

title: Strings are immutable
question: Can you modify a string in place? What does converting it to []byte do?
answer: No, strings are immutable. []byte(s) copies the bytes into a new array you can change without touching s. Assigning a string copies only its (pointer, length) header, which is safe because nothing can change the bytes; s += " world" builds a new string and repoints s.
watch: Watch the conversion allocate a separate byte array, and s += create new bytes while t still points at the old ones.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := "hello"
	b := []byte(s)
	b[0] = 'J'
	fmt.Println(s, string(b))

	t := s
	s += " world"
	fmt.Println(t, s)
}

title: An interface holds a type and a value
question: What is stored inside an interface value, and when are two interfaces equal?
answer: An interface value is a pair: a dynamic type and a value of that type. Two interfaces are equal only if both the types and the values are equal, so an interface holding int 1 and one holding int64 1 differ. An interface is nil only when both halves are empty; holding a nil *int still gives it a type, so it is not nil.
watch: Watch each interface box show its type next to its value; c has type *int with a nil value inside.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var a any = 1
	var b any = int64(1)
	fmt.Println(a == b)
	fmt.Printf("%T %T\n", a, b)
	var one any = 1
	fmt.Println(a == one)

	var p *int
	var c any = p
	fmt.Println(c == nil, p == nil)
}

title: Generic constraints and ~
question: Write a generic Sum that works for int, float64 and your own named integer types. What does ~ do in a constraint?
answer: A constraint lists the allowed type set (written inline here, or as a named interface such as type Number interface{ ~int | ~float64 }); ~int means "any type whose underlying type is int", so a named type like Cents is accepted while a plain int union would reject it. The compiler checks that + is valid for every type in the set, and T is inferred from the argument at each call.
watch: Watch each call instantiate Sum with a different T, shown in the frame header.

title: errors.Is and errors.As through wrapping
question: How do you check for a specific error once it has been wrapped with fmt.Errorf("%w")?
answer: %w keeps the original error inside the new one, so == against the sentinel fails but errors.Is walks the Unwrap chain and finds it. errors.As walks the same chain looking for an error of a given type and, if found, stores it in the target pointer so you can read its fields.
watch: Watch each wrapper error on the heap keep a pointer to the error it wraps; Is and As follow that pointer.
expected:
load user: not found
false true
query was id=7

title: Defer can change a named result
question: Can a deferred function change what a function returns?
answer: Yes, if the result is named. return 3 first assigns 3 to n, then deferred calls run, then the function returns n, so the defer doubles it to 6. With an unnamed result the return value is copied out before the defer runs, so changing a local afterwards has no effect.
watch: Watch the result slot in double's frame: it holds 3 at return, then becomes 6 when the defer runs.

title: Turning a panic into an error
question: How do you stop a panic from crashing the program and report it as an error?
answer: Call recover inside a deferred function. A panic unwinds the stack running deferred calls; if one of them calls recover, the panic stops and recover returns the panic value, so the defer can set a named error result. recover returns nil when called anywhere else, such as directly in normal code.
watch: Watch the divide panic start unwinding safeDiv, the deferred function catch it, and the err slot get filled before returning normally.
expected:
5 <nil>
0 recovered: runtime error: integer divide by zero

title: recover cannot catch another goroutine's panic
question: main has a deferred recover. Does it catch a panic that happens in a goroutine main started?
answer: No. recover only stops a panic in the goroutine that is panicking, and only from a function that goroutine deferred. A panic that reaches the top of any goroutine crashes the whole program, so each goroutine that might panic needs its own deferred recover.
watch: Watch the worker goroutine unwind with no deferred calls of its own; main's defer never runs before the program dies.

title: Buffered vs unbuffered channels
question: What is the difference between a buffered and an unbuffered channel?
answer: An unbuffered channel has no storage: a send blocks until a receiver takes the value, so the two goroutines meet at that point. A buffered channel with capacity n lets up to n sends complete with no receiver; the sender only blocks when the buffer is full and the receiver when it is empty. len reports values waiting in the buffer and cap its size.
watch: Watch the buffered channel's slots fill with 1 and 2, then main block on the unbuffered send until the receiver goroutine arrives.
source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	buf := make(chan int, 2)
	buf <- 1
	buf <- 2 // no receiver needed: fits in the buffer
	fmt.Println("buffered:", len(buf), cap(buf))

	unbuf := make(chan int)
	done := make(chan bool)
	go func() {
		fmt.Println("receiver got", <-unbuf)
		done <- true
	}()
	unbuf <- 3 // blocks until the goroutine receives
	<-done
	fmt.Println("unbuffered:", len(unbuf), cap(unbuf))
}

title: Who closes, and how range ends
question: How does a for-range loop over a channel know when to stop, and who should close the channel?
answer: range keeps receiving until the channel is closed and drained, then the loop ends. The sender closes, because only the sender knows no more values are coming; closing from the receiver side risks a send on a closed channel, which panics. Without the close, the range would block forever.
watch: Watch the producer send three values, close the channel, and the range loop exit once the channel is closed and empty.

title: Non-blocking send and receive
question: How do you try to send or receive on a channel without blocking?
answer: Use select with a default case. If no other case can proceed right now, default runs immediately instead of blocking. Here the buffer holds one value, so the first send succeeds, later sends fall through to default, and a receive from an empty channel does too.
watch: Watch the one-slot buffer: the first send fills it, the next two take the default branch.

full, dropped 1

title: Timing out a receive
question: How do you stop waiting on a channel after a timeout?
answer: select on both the channel and a timer channel such as time.After(d); whichever is ready first wins. Here nothing is ever sent, so the timer fires and the timeout branch runs. In long-running loops prefer a context or a reused time.Timer so you can cancel the wait explicitly.
watch: Watch main park on both cases until the timer delivers on its channel.

title: Nil channels disable select cases
question: You are merging two channels with select. How do you stop reading from one after it closes?
answer: Set that channel variable to nil. A receive from a nil channel blocks forever, so its select case can never be chosen, while a closed channel would be ready every time and spin. The loop ends when both have been set to nil.
watch: Watch a and b turn nil one by one after they close, and select stop considering them.

title: Waiting for goroutines with WaitGroup
question: How do you wait for a group of goroutines to finish, and where must wg.Add be called?
answer: Call wg.Add before starting each goroutine, have the goroutine call wg.Done when it finishes (usually with defer), and call wg.Wait to block until the counter reaches zero. Add must happen before the go statement, otherwise Wait can see zero and return early; Go 1.25 also added wg.Go, which does the Add and Done for you. Each goroutine writes its own index, so no lock is needed.
watch: Watch the WaitGroup counter rise to 5, fall as each goroutine finishes, and main wake at zero.

title: Protecting shared state with a Mutex
question: Several goroutines increment one counter. Why is n++ unsafe and how do you fix it?
answer: n++ is a read, an add and a write; two goroutines can read the same value and one update is lost, which is a data race. Holding a sync.Mutex around the increment means only one goroutine runs it at a time, so every update is kept. The mutex lives next to the data, and the methods use a pointer receiver so the mutex is never copied.
watch: Watch goroutines queue on the mutex: only the holder touches n, the rest wait until Unlock.

title: A goroutine leaked by a blocked send
question: What is a goroutine leak, and how does one happen with an unbuffered channel?
answer: A leak is a goroutine that can never finish, so it and everything it references stay in memory forever; the garbage collector does not reclaim blocked goroutines. Here each start call launches a goroutine that sends on an unbuffered channel nobody will ever receive from, so all three stay blocked. Fix it by giving the channel a buffer of 1, making sure someone receives, or cancelling with a context.
watch: Watch three goroutines park on their sends and stay blocked after start returns each time.

title: Stopping a worker with context
question: How do you tell a running goroutine to stop?
answer: Pass it a context.Context and have it select on ctx.Done() next to its normal work. Calling cancel closes the Done channel, which makes that case ready in every goroutine watching it, and ctx.Err() then reports context.Canceled. The worker returns on its own; Go has no way to kill a goroutine from outside.
watch: Watch the worker take two jobs, then the Done channel close on cancel and the worker return.

job 1
job 2
worker stopped: context canceled
main exits

title: Fan-out, fan-in worker pool
question: Build a worker pool: several workers read jobs from one channel and send results to another. How do you know when all results are in?
answer: Workers range over the jobs channel, so closing jobs makes them all exit after the work runs out. A separate goroutine waits on a WaitGroup for every worker and then closes results, which ends main's range over results. Results arrive in any order, so combine them in an order-independent way.
watch: Watch the three workers pull jobs from one channel and push into results, then the closer goroutine close results after the last worker is done.
